rows.label: Concept
rows.text: The **relative refractive index** of medium 2 with respect to medium 1 is $n_{21} = n_2/n_1 = v_1/v_2 = \sin i/\sin r$; reversing the media simply inverts it ($n_{12} = 1/n_{21}$), and absolute indices (measured against vacuum) chain through any number of media. A direct consequence is **apparent depth**: looking vertically into a medium of index n, depths shrink by the factor n — apparent depth = real depth/n.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - n₂₁ = n₂/n₁ = v₁/v₂ - Apparent depth = real depth/n - n₁₂ = 1/n₂₁

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Apparent depth = real/n** — the fish looks *shallower* (closer to the surface), not deeper.  ·  **Relative vs absolute:** n₂₁ = n₂/n₁; absolute indices are measured against vacuum.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "The relative refractive index of medium 2 with respect to medium 1 is the ratio of the absolute refractive index of 2 to that of 1."

rows.label: Solved

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Chaining Media Together Light travels from water into glass — how do their refractive indices combine? The relation between refractive indices lets you jump between any pair of media using air (or vacuum) as the common currency, and it explains why pools look shallow and spearfishing takes aim below the target.  ·  ## 2. rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: "Divide by n looking down into water; multiply looking from water up."

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **Numerical (3m): A coin lies at the bottom of a 3 m deep water tank (n = 4/3). Find its apparent depth.** — apparent = 3/(4/3) = 2.25 m — the coin seems 2.25 m below the surface.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Quote the direction of view in the answer — 'appears raised to an observer above'.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **The Snell's-law constant IS the relative refractive index** — one quantity, several faces.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: n₂₁ = n₂/n₁ = v₁/v₂ = sin i/sin r; n₁₂ = 1/n₂₁.  ·  Looking into water, objects appear raised by factor n.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: A pool 2 m deep looks only ~1.5 m deep through the water — the classic apparent-depth illusion.
